title: Genetics & Breeding
learningOutcome: Understand genotype, phenotype, inheritance, chemotype, sex expression, population structure and modern molecular tools well enough to design crosses, measure offspring, select parents and describe a line without turning labels or generation numbers into guarantees.
evidenceBoundary: Cannabis traits range from relatively simple genetic effects to highly polygenic, environmentally responsive outcomes. Pedigree names, sativa/indica labels, generation labels, markers and one exceptional phenotype are evidence of different kinds; none alone proves stable performance.

chapters.title: Genotype, Phenotype & Environment
chapters.objective: Separate inherited genetic variation from the phenotype produced when that genotype develops in a particular environment.

lessons.title: Genotype is not the visible plant
lessons.summary: A genotype is the inherited DNA combination; phenotype is the observed result of that genotype developing through a specific environment, developmental stage and history.
lessons.cultivation: Describe traits as observations under known conditions rather than fixed promises attached to a seed name.
lessons.observe: Record plant ID, family, environment, stage and exact trait measurement together.

lessons.title: Phenotypic plasticity can hide or exaggerate genetic differences
lessons.summary: Internode length, branching, flowering time, color and stress response can shift with light, temperature, roots and other environmental conditions.
lessons.cultivation: Compare relatives under as similar conditions as practical before declaring a difference genetic.
lessons.observe: Preserve environmental records and replicate observations across plants or runs when selecting.

lessons.title: Heritability is population- and environment-specific
lessons.summary: A trait can be strongly inherited in one population and environment yet less predictive elsewhere; heritability is not a universal percentage permanently attached to the trait.
lessons.cultivation: Use family data and repeated evaluation rather than treating a published heritability estimate as a guarantee.
lessons.observe: Track within-family and between-family variation under the same evaluation design.

lessons.title: Selection changes a population through who reproduces
lessons.summary: Breeding progress comes from choosing parents based on defined traits and transmitting favorable genetic combinations while managing unwanted correlated traits and diversity loss.
lessons.cultivation: Write selection objectives before choosing parents so memorable plants do not replace a consistent standard.
lessons.observe: Record why each parent was selected, rejected traits and which evidence supports the decision.

chapters.title: Population Structure, Lineage & Genetic Identity
chapters.objective: Understand why commercial names, ancestry labels and pedigrees are useful records but are not substitutes for genetic characterization.

lessons.title: Cannabis contains broad and admixed genetic diversity
lessons.summary: Genome-wide studies distinguish major population histories, yet modern breeding has mixed ancestry extensively across drug-type and hemp-derived material.
lessons.cultivation: Treat ancestry as a continuum and documented pedigree rather than forcing every plant into a simplistic binary label.
lessons.observe: Record verified parentage and source while separating it from appearance-based ancestry claims.

lessons.title: Sativa and indica labels do not reliably encode genome-wide identity
lessons.summary: Commercial ancestry labels may correlate only partially with measured genetic structure, and strain names can be reused across unrelated material.
lessons.cultivation: Use cultivar or line name as an identifier, not proof of genetic composition or effect.
lessons.observe: Keep breeder source, accession, generation and parent IDs with the name.

lessons.title: Pedigrees are hypotheses that improve with records
lessons.summary: A written cross describes intended parents, but mix-ups, stray pollen and mislabeled seed can break the assumed lineage.
lessons.cultivation: Protect breeding credibility with controlled pollination, labels and retained records rather than memory.
lessons.observe: Record parent IDs, pollination date and method, isolation, seed lot and any uncertainty.

lessons.title: Genetic diversity is a resource and a constraint
lessons.summary: Narrow selection can increase uniformity but also remove alleles useful for vigor, disease resistance or future objectives; broad populations carry more variation but require more selection.
lessons.cultivation: Match population breadth to the breeding goal instead of maximizing either uniformity or diversity blindly.
lessons.observe: Track family size, number of parents retained, repeated crosses and signs of reduced vigor.

chapters.title: Inheritance, Segregation & Generations
chapters.objective: Use Mendelian expectations where appropriate while recognizing polygenic traits, linkage, epistasis and environmental variance.

lessons.title: F1 uniformity depends on parent genetics
lessons.summary: An F1 from highly homozygous parents can be relatively uniform, while crosses involving heterozygous parents can produce substantial variation immediately.
lessons.cultivation: Do not promise F1 uniformity without knowing the parental genetic structure.
lessons.observe: Record parent stability, number of offspring evaluated and the distribution of key traits.

lessons.title: F2 populations reveal hidden segregation
lessons.summary: Selfing or intercrossing F1 individuals reshuffles alleles and often increases visible variation, making F2 populations useful for selection but less predictable plant to plant.
lessons.cultivation: Use enough F2 individuals to see the range relevant to the breeding objective rather than judging the family from a few plants.
lessons.observe: Record trait frequencies, extremes, family size and selection intensity.

lessons.title: Backcrossing increases resemblance at selected loci, not whole-genome identity
lessons.summary: Repeated crossing to a recurrent parent increases its expected genomic contribution, but recombination and selection determine which regions and traits are retained.
lessons.cultivation: Define which donor trait is being recovered and which recurrent-parent traits must be restored.
lessons.observe: Track generation, recurrent parent, donor-trait evidence and off-target traits each cycle.

lessons.title: Many useful traits are not single-gene traits
lessons.summary: Yield, architecture, aroma intensity, flowering time and stress tolerance can involve many loci plus environment, linkage and gene interactions.
lessons.cultivation: Use repeated phenotyping and family comparison for complex traits instead of assuming simple segregation ratios.
lessons.observe: Measure quantitative traits continuously and compare distributions, not just pass/fail labels.

chapters.title: Chemotype & Cannabinoid Genetics
chapters.objective: Connect classical chemotype segregation with modern knowledge of THCAS/CBDAS loci while avoiding deterministic potency predictions.

lessons.title: Chemotype describes relative cannabinoid-acid pattern
lessons.summary: Type I, II and III classifications reflect THC-dominant, intermediate and CBD-dominant profiles, but final concentration also depends on development and environment.
lessons.cultivation: Use chemotype to describe pathway tendency, not to promise a fixed potency value.
lessons.observe: Measure the actual harvested material when cannabinoid concentration matters.

lessons.title: Classical crosses revealed predictable chemotype segregation
lessons.summary: Controlled crosses demonstrated inheritance patterns consistent with codominant chemotype factors, helping establish a genetic basis for THC/CBD ratio.
lessons.cultivation: Use expected ratios as models to test with offspring data rather than excuses to skip testing.
lessons.observe: Record offspring chemotype counts and compare observed versus expected segregation.

lessons.title: Modern assemblies show the synthase region is structurally complex
lessons.summary: THCAS and CBDAS occur in repetitive, rearranged genomic regions with copy and functional variation, so modern genetics is more complex than the earliest one-locus model.
lessons.cultivation: Avoid treating one marker as perfect across all germplasm unless it has been validated in the specific breeding material.
lessons.observe: Compare marker calls with measured chemotype and investigate discordant plants.

lessons.title: Genotype predicts pathway potential better than final concentration
lessons.summary: Genes constrain what chemistry can be produced, while total cannabinoid accumulation changes with genotype, flower development, environment and analytical method.
lessons.cultivation: Separate breeding for chemotype identity from breeding for quantitative concentration and agronomic performance.
lessons.observe: Track genetic or marker data, harvest stage, lab method and concentration as separate variables.

chapters.title: Sex Determination & Sex Expression
chapters.objective: Distinguish chromosomal sex determination from plastic expression of male and female flowers under genetic, hormonal, developmental and environmental influences.

lessons.title: Cannabis is predominantly dioecious with sex chromosomes
lessons.summary: Dioecious cannabis commonly follows an XX/XY system, creating a strong chromosomal basis for sex while other regulatory layers influence floral expression.
lessons.cultivation: Keep chromosomal sex and observed floral phenotype conceptually separate.
lessons.observe: Record sex-marker result when used, visible floral structures and developmental stage.

lessons.title: Sex expression is biologically plastic
lessons.summary: Female-genotype plants can express male flowers under some genetic, hormonal or environmental contexts, and the degree of instability varies among genotypes.
lessons.cultivation: Do not describe every intersex event as proof of one environmental cause or one inherited defect.
lessons.observe: Record lineage, flower location, timing, stress history and frequency across relatives.

lessons.title: Induced masculinization is a breeding tool with mechanism
lessons.summary: Ethylene-inhibiting treatments can induce male flowers on genetically female plants for feminized-seed production, but treatment and plant response require controlled practice and legal or safety compliance.
lessons.cultivation: Treat induced sex reversal as a managed breeding procedure, not evidence that spontaneous instability is desirable.
lessons.observe: Record treated plant, controlled treatment protocol, pollen fertility and offspring evaluation.

lessons.title: Early sex markers are tools, not complete breeding decisions
lessons.summary: Molecular markers can identify sex-linked sequences before flowering, but marker performance depends on assay validation and germplasm background.
lessons.cultivation: Validate markers against known plants and keep phenotype confirmation in the quality system.
lessons.observe: Record assay, controls, result, later floral sex and any discordance.

chapters.title: Phenotyping, Selection & Parent Choice
chapters.objective: Convert breeding goals into measured selection criteria and choose parents from replicated evidence rather than one impressive plant.

lessons.title: A breeding objective should name the trait and tradeoff
lessons.summary: Selecting for earlier flowering, compact architecture, disease tolerance or chemistry can shift other traits through linkage or correlated biology.
lessons.cultivation: Define must-have, preferred and disqualifying traits before evaluation starts.
lessons.observe: Use the same scoring rubric across candidates and preserve rejected-trait notes.

lessons.title: Quantitative phenotyping makes selection repeatable
lessons.summary: Height, internode length, flowering time, yield, chemical concentration and disease incidence are more comparable when measured with defined methods.
lessons.cultivation: Write how each trait is measured before seeing the results to reduce subjective drift.
lessons.observe: Record units, timing, instrument or method and raw values before scores.

lessons.title: Replicated performance separates signal from one-environment luck
lessons.summary: A plant can look exceptional because of a favorable local environment; relatives or clones tested across runs provide stronger evidence of stable performance.
lessons.cultivation: Retest high-value selections when possible before committing a breeding program around them.
lessons.observe: Compare clone or relative performance across positions, runs or environments with the same trait definitions.

lessons.title: Parent choice should preserve complementary strengths
lessons.summary: Crosses are designed to combine traits, expose recessives or test hypotheses; choosing two similar favorites without a stated purpose can reduce information gained.
lessons.cultivation: Write what each parent contributes and what outcome would falsify the crossing hypothesis.
lessons.observe: Keep parent phenotype, marker data where available, family performance and cross rationale together.

chapters.title: Stabilization, Testing & Line Development
chapters.objective: Track line development through generations using family-level data, controlled mating and explicit release criteria instead of generation labels alone.

lessons.title: Generation labels describe history, not quality
lessons.summary: F2, F3 or F5 tells how many breeding cycles occurred but does not prove uniformity, stability, vigor or trait fixation.
lessons.cultivation: Publish generation together with what was actually selected and observed.
lessons.observe: Record population size, selection method, parent structure and trait variation each generation.

lessons.title: Family selection preserves useful information
lessons.summary: Tracking full-sib, half-sib or selfed families shows which parents repeatedly transmit desired traits and which apparent elites fail in their offspring.
lessons.cultivation: Evaluate parent quality partly by offspring performance instead of only the parent's phenotype.
lessons.observe: Link every offspring to family and compare family means, spread and defect frequencies.

lessons.title: Uniformity must be defined trait by trait
lessons.summary: A line can be uniform for sex or chemotype while still variable for height, aroma, flowering time or yield.
lessons.cultivation: Choose the traits that must be consistent for the intended release and tolerate variation only where acceptable.
lessons.observe: Quantify variation for each release-critical trait across an adequate sample.

lessons.title: Release decisions should include negative traits
lessons.summary: Intersex expression, weak roots, disease susceptibility, poor structure or unstable chemistry can outweigh attractive aroma or appearance.
lessons.cultivation: Maintain explicit disqualifiers and do not erase them from records when a plant excels elsewhere.
lessons.observe: Track defect frequency by family and generation, including plants that were removed.

chapters.title: Molecular Tools, Records & Breeding Evidence
chapters.objective: Use markers, genomic resources and breeding records as complementary evidence while keeping functional validation and phenotype central.

lessons.title: Markers are linked evidence, not the trait itself
lessons.summary: A DNA marker can predict an allele or genomic region, but recombination, population differences and assay error can weaken the relationship.
lessons.cultivation: Validate marker-trait associations in the actual breeding material before using them as sole culling rules.
lessons.observe: Record marker assay, genotype call, phenotype and discordant cases.

lessons.title: Pangenomes expose variation a single reference can miss
lessons.summary: Cannabis pangenomic resources capture presence/absence and structural variation across diverse accessions, reducing the assumption that one reference genome contains every relevant sequence.
lessons.cultivation: Use modern genomic resources to generate hypotheses while keeping breeding decisions connected to measured traits.
lessons.observe: Document reference or resource version and the population in which a candidate association was discovered.

lessons.title: Genomic selection requires good phenotype data
lessons.summary: Prediction models can use many markers at once, but model quality depends on representative training populations and accurate phenotyping.
lessons.cultivation: Treat genomic prediction as a model that must be validated, not an oracle that replaces crop evaluation.
lessons.observe: Track prediction accuracy, population relatedness and real offspring performance.

lessons.title: Breeding records are part of genetic quality
lessons.summary: Accurate parent IDs, seed-lot labels, generation history, selection notes, photos and test results preserve the evidence needed to reproduce or audit a line.
lessons.cultivation: Use stable IDs and immutable cross or seed-lot records so naming changes do not destroy lineage evidence.
lessons.observe: Audit whether every released lot can be traced to parents, generation, selection criteria and retained evidence.
